subject: Technology

sources.title: NZC Technology Years 0–10, September 2026
sources.status: published-final; Gazette pending; proposed Years 9–10 from 2027, Years 0–8 from 2029; transition applies

topics.name: Designing for a need
topics.description: People design and make things to respond to needs or solve problems. A useful idea considers who will use the outcome and why.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: designing for a need.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: To protect the toy from a chosen condition, such as pretend rain, in a suitable model.
misconceptions: A design is useful without considering what it is for.
topics.question: Why might someone design a shelter for a toy?
topics.answer: To protect the toy from a chosen condition, such as pretend rain, in a suitable model.
topics.explanation: People design and make things to respond to needs or solve problems. A useful idea considers who will use the outcome and why.
hints: Who or what is the design for?
What problem should the shelter address?
topics.activity: Draw two ideas for a small paper shelter and explain the need each addresses.

topics.name: Following a making sequence
topics.description: A design process can involve planning, making, testing and improving in an appropriate order.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: following a making sequence.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Testing provides information about whether the bridge meets its intended purpose.
misconceptions: A design cannot be changed after the first attempt.
topics.question: Why might a maker test a paper bridge after assembling it?
topics.answer: Testing provides information about whether the bridge meets its intended purpose.
topics.explanation: A design process can involve planning, making, testing and improving in an appropriate order.
hints: What does the maker need to find out?
How could trying the model provide evidence?
topics.activity: Fold a paper bridge, test it with a light object in a safe space and suggest one improvement.

topics.name: Using a design brief
topics.description: A design brief describes a need and criteria that can help a maker develop and evaluate an outcome.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 2 > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: using a design brief.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Whether the holder remains upright with the intended pencils in it.
misconceptions: A design brief is unrelated to how a finished outcome is evaluated.
topics.question: A brief says a pencil holder should stand securely. What could be tested?
topics.answer: Whether the holder remains upright with the intended pencils in it.
topics.explanation: A design brief describes a need and criteria that can help a maker develop and evaluate an outcome.
hints: What does the brief require?
What simple test would check that requirement?
topics.activity: Write two criteria for a cardboard holder and sketch a safe way to test each one.

topics.name: Design choices and environmental impacts
topics.description: Material choices can affect a product's usefulness and environmental impact. Comparing options requires considering how an item is used, maintained and disposed of.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 2 > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: design choices and environmental impacts.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Their impacts depend on materials, number of uses and other lifecycle factors.
misconceptions: A label such as reusable automatically proves an option has the lowest impact in every situation.
topics.question: Why compare reusable and single-use packaging before choosing one?
topics.answer: Their impacts depend on materials, number of uses and other lifecycle factors.
topics.explanation: Material choices can affect a product's usefulness and environmental impact. Comparing options requires considering how an item is used, maintained and disposed of.
hints: How many times might each option be used?
What happens after use?
topics.activity: Compare two fictional packages and list what information would be needed to judge their impacts.

topics.name: Users, criteria and constraints
topics.description: A design responds to user needs while working within constraints such as available materials, time and safety requirements.
topics.locator: PDF p. 13, Phase 3 > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: users, criteria and constraints.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Their input helps establish whether the outcome will be useful and accessible for its intended purpose.
misconceptions: A designer's preference is the only information needed for a useful outcome.
topics.question: Why ask a user about their needs before choosing a design?
topics.answer: Their input helps establish whether the outcome will be useful and accessible for its intended purpose.
topics.explanation: A design responds to user needs while working within constraints such as available materials, time and safety requirements.
hints: Who will use the outcome?
What can that person tell the designer?
topics.activity: Plan a fictional storage solution and list one user need, one criterion and one constraint.

topics.name: Intended and unintended effects
topics.description: A technological outcome can create benefits and unintended effects for different people and environments.
topics.locator: PDF p. 13, Phase 3 > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: intended and unintended effects.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The notifications might distract some users, depending on how the app is used and configured.
misconceptions: Technology has only the effects its designer intended.
topics.question: A messaging app helps people communicate but sends frequent notifications. What is a possible unintended effect?
topics.answer: The notifications might distract some users, depending on how the app is used and configured.
topics.explanation: A technological outcome can create benefits and unintended effects for different people and environments.
hints: What was the intended benefit?
What other effect might result from frequent alerts?
topics.activity: For a fictional technology, list one intended benefit, one possible unintended effect and a question to investigate.

topics.name: Selecting materials for performance
topics.description: Material properties such as strength, flexibility and absorbency affect whether a material suits an intended use.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 3 > Materials Technology (Resistant and Textiles); broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: selecting materials for performance.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Fabric can bend with the pouch without easily breaking, although other criteria also matter.
misconceptions: All materials perform equally well for every purpose.
topics.question: Why might flexible fabric suit a soft pouch better than brittle material?
topics.answer: Fabric can bend with the pouch without easily breaking, although other criteria also matter.
topics.explanation: Material properties such as strength, flexibility and absorbency affect whether a material suits an intended use.
hints: What movement must the pouch tolerate?
Which material can bend without crumbling?
topics.activity: Compare safe material samples for a fictional pouch and justify a choice using two properties.

topics.name: Joining materials for a purpose
topics.description: Different joins, such as folding, stitching or adhesive, suit different materials and forces. Safe testing can help compare them.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 3 > Materials Technology (Resistant and Textiles); broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: joining materials for a purpose.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: A small test can reveal whether the join holds and whether the materials work together.
misconceptions: One joining method is best for all materials and loads.
topics.question: Why test a join on scrap material before making a final item?
topics.answer: A small test can reveal whether the join holds and whether the materials work together.
topics.explanation: Different joins, such as folding, stitching or adhesive, suit different materials and forces. Safe testing can help compare them.
hints: What could go wrong with an untested join?
How can a small sample provide evidence?
topics.activity: Use paper folding or a safe adhesive with supervision to compare two joins for a light paper model.

topics.name: Ingredients and sensory attributes
topics.description: Ingredients and processing methods can affect a food outcome's flavour, appearance and texture. Food handling must be safe and suitable for participants.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Phase 3 > Food and Processing Technology; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: ingredients and sensory attributes.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It can make the mixture smoother, depending on the ingredients and processing.
misconceptions: Ingredients and processing have no effect on a food's texture.
topics.question: How could blending change the texture of a soft food?
topics.answer: It can make the mixture smoother, depending on the ingredients and processing.
topics.explanation: Ingredients and processing methods can affect a food outcome's flavour, appearance and texture. Food handling must be safe and suitable for participants.
hints: Compare whole pieces with a blended mixture.
What happens to the size of the pieces?
topics.activity: Plan a fictional food product and describe how one processing method could change texture; account for allergies and safe handling.

topics.name: Hygiene in food preparation
topics.description: Safe food preparation involves appropriate hygiene, clean equipment and attention to ingredients and individual needs.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Phase 3 > Food and Processing Technology; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: hygiene in food preparation.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It helps reduce contamination and supports safer food handling.
misconceptions: Cleanliness is only about how a finished food looks.
topics.question: Why clean equipment before preparing food?
topics.answer: It helps reduce contamination and supports safer food handling.
topics.explanation: Safe food preparation involves appropriate hygiene, clean equipment and attention to ingredients and individual needs.
hints: What might remain on unclean equipment?
Could that material transfer to food?
topics.activity: Make a checklist for a fictional food activity covering handwashing, clean equipment and allergies.

topics.name: Inputs, processes and outputs
topics.description: A system takes inputs, performs processes and produces outputs. Its parts work together for a purpose.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 3 > Systems and Control; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: inputs, processes and outputs.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The battery supplies electrical energy and the torch produces light when switched on.
misconceptions: A system's output is unrelated to its inputs.
topics.question: In a simple torch, what input and output can be identified?
topics.answer: The battery supplies electrical energy and the torch produces light when switched on.
topics.explanation: A system takes inputs, performs processes and produces outputs. Its parts work together for a purpose.
hints: What supplies energy?
What does the torch produce?
topics.activity: Draw a labelled input–process–output diagram for a familiar non-mains device.

topics.name: Feedback in a control system
topics.description: A control system can use feedback about its output to adjust its operation towards a target.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 3 > Systems and Control; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: feedback in a control system.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It may signal the heater to operate, depending on the system.
misconceptions: Feedback cannot influence how a system operates.
topics.question: A thermostat detects that a room is cooler than its target. What might it signal?
topics.answer: It may signal the heater to operate, depending on the system.
topics.explanation: A control system can use feedback about its output to adjust its operation towards a target.
hints: What information is measured?
How could the system respond to the difference from the target?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional temperature-control loop showing target, measurement and adjustment.

topics.name: Algorithms as ordered instructions
topics.description: An algorithm is a sequence of instructions for a task. The instructions need enough detail to be followed and tested.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 3 > Digital Technology; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: algorithms as ordered instructions.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Changing the order can produce a different or unsuccessful result, such as packing it before adding the filling.
misconceptions: Instructions give the same result regardless of their order.
topics.question: Why does the order of instructions matter when making a sandwich?
topics.answer: Changing the order can produce a different or unsuccessful result, such as packing it before adding the filling.
topics.explanation: An algorithm is a sequence of instructions for a task. The instructions need enough detail to be followed and tested.
hints: What must happen before the sandwich is complete?
Try changing the order of two steps.
topics.activity: Write and test instructions for arranging three paper shapes, then revise any ambiguous step.

topics.name: Testing and debugging
topics.description: Testing compares a digital outcome with the intended behaviour; debugging identifies and corrects a cause of an error.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 3 > Digital Technology; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: testing and debugging.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Check the operation used and test again with known inputs.
misconceptions: A program that runs without crashing must always give the correct result.
topics.question: A program should add two numbers but subtracts them. What should be checked?
topics.answer: Check the operation used and test again with known inputs.
topics.explanation: Testing compares a digital outcome with the intended behaviour; debugging identifies and corrects a cause of an error.
hints: What result is intended?
Which operation produces that result?
topics.activity: Use a paper flowchart with an intentional wrong operation, find the error and test a corrected version.

topics.name: Evaluating design trade-offs
topics.description: Technological decisions can balance user needs, accessibility, cost, safety and environmental effects. Evidence helps justify trade-offs.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Phase 4 > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: evaluating design trade-offs.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Investigate accessibility and compare alternatives, costs and user feedback before choosing.
misconceptions: The cheapest design is automatically the best for every user.
topics.question: A design is inexpensive but difficult for some users to operate. What should the team consider?
topics.answer: Investigate accessibility and compare alternatives, costs and user feedback before choosing.
topics.explanation: Technological decisions can balance user needs, accessibility, cost, safety and environmental effects. Evidence helps justify trade-offs.
hints: Who may be affected by the difficulty?
What evidence could help compare alternatives?
topics.activity: Compare two fictional designs against a short set of user, safety and environmental criteria.

topics.name: Data, consent and responsible design
topics.description: Designers should consider how data is collected, governed and used, including privacy, consent and relevant cultural responsibilities.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Phase 4 > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: data, consent and responsible design.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Collecting less information can reduce unnecessary exposure and helps designers consider privacy and purpose.
misconceptions: Collecting more personal information is always necessary for better design.
topics.question: Why ask whether data collection is necessary for a digital feature?
topics.answer: Collecting less information can reduce unnecessary exposure and helps designers consider privacy and purpose.
topics.explanation: Designers should consider how data is collected, governed and used, including privacy, consent and relevant cultural responsibilities.
hints: What is the feature trying to do?
Does it require every piece of information requested?
topics.activity: Review a fictional app form and suggest one unnecessary field to remove and one consent question.

topics.name: Representing three-dimensional design ideas
topics.description: Design drawings and models represent the form, dimensions and perspective of an intended outcome for an audience.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 4 > Spatial and Product Design; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: representing three-dimensional design ideas.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The sketch helps communicate appearance while dimensions help communicate size and construction details.
misconceptions: One drawing always communicates every aspect of a design equally well.
topics.question: Why might a designer use both a perspective sketch and a dimensioned view?
topics.answer: The sketch helps communicate appearance while dimensions help communicate size and construction details.
topics.explanation: Design drawings and models represent the form, dimensions and perspective of an intended outcome for an audience.
hints: What can the viewer see in a perspective view?
What additional information do dimensions provide?
topics.activity: Sketch a simple fictional storage box from one viewpoint and add a separate labelled dimensioned view.

topics.name: Designing for access
topics.description: Product and spatial design can consider different users, capabilities and contexts. Testing with appropriate users can reveal barriers.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 4 > Spatial and Product Design; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: designing for access.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Feedback may reveal readability or usability barriers the designer did not anticipate.
misconceptions: A design is accessible to everyone if it works for its creator.
topics.question: Why test a control label with people who have different access needs?
topics.answer: Feedback may reveal readability or usability barriers the designer did not anticipate.
topics.explanation: Product and spatial design can consider different users, capabilities and contexts. Testing with appropriate users can reveal barriers.
hints: Who might use the control?
What could make the label difficult to read or operate?
topics.activity: Review a fictional control panel for readable labels, contrast and clear action descriptions, then propose one improvement.

topics.name: Material lifecycle and design
topics.description: Material selection can consider performance, repair, reuse, waste and other impacts over an outcome's lifecycle.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 4 > Materials Technology (Resistant and Textiles); broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: material lifecycle and design.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Its full impact depends on materials, production, use, repair and disposal as well as durability.
misconceptions: Durability alone proves a material has the lowest overall environmental impact.
topics.question: Why might a durable item still need a lifecycle assessment?
topics.answer: Its full impact depends on materials, production, use, repair and disposal as well as durability.
topics.explanation: Material selection can consider performance, repair, reuse, waste and other impacts over an outcome's lifecycle.
hints: What happens before the product is used?
What happens after it is worn out?
topics.activity: Compare two fictional materials for a product and list evidence needed to assess performance and lifecycle impacts.

topics.name: Choosing joins for a load
topics.description: A join must be suitable for the materials and the forces it will experience. Designers can test a model safely before selecting a method.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 4 > Materials Technology (Resistant and Textiles); broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: choosing joins for a load.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The shelf join must carry a greater load and suit the materials and expected use.
misconceptions: A join that holds paper will necessarily support any load.
topics.question: Why might a join for a loaded shelf need different consideration from a paper label?
topics.answer: The shelf join must carry a greater load and suit the materials and expected use.
topics.explanation: A join must be suitable for the materials and the forces it will experience. Designers can test a model safely before selecting a method.
hints: What force acts on the shelf join?
Is the paper label expected to carry the same load?
topics.activity: Compare two fictional joins on paper and identify what additional testing a real loaded object would need.

topics.name: Processing methods and food outcomes
topics.description: Food processing methods can change properties such as texture, flavour and shelf life. Safe handling and reliable guidance are essential.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 4 > Food and Processing Technology; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: processing methods and food outcomes.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Removing some moisture can change texture and influence storage properties; safety depends on the food and method.
misconceptions: Processing never changes a food's properties.
topics.question: How could drying affect a food outcome?
topics.answer: Removing some moisture can change texture and influence storage properties; safety depends on the food and method.
topics.explanation: Food processing methods can change properties such as texture, flavour and shelf life. Safe handling and reliable guidance are essential.
hints: What does drying remove?
How might less moisture change the product?
topics.activity: Compare labelled examples of fresh and dried food and describe a difference; do not attempt preservation without appropriate guidance.

topics.name: Evaluating a food design
topics.description: A food outcome can be evaluated against intended sensory attributes, user needs, safety and cultural or environmental considerations.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 4 > Food and Processing Technology; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: evaluating a food design.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Ingredients that are safe for one person may be unsuitable for another, so needs must be checked.
misconceptions: A food product is fit for every user if it tastes appealing.
topics.question: Why consider allergies when planning a food outcome?
topics.answer: Ingredients that are safe for one person may be unsuitable for another, so needs must be checked.
topics.explanation: A food outcome can be evaluated against intended sensory attributes, user needs, safety and cultural or environmental considerations.
hints: Can every person eat the same ingredients?
What information is needed before serving food?
topics.activity: Create a fictional food brief with a texture goal and a safety requirement, and explain how each would be checked.

topics.name: Using feedback to improve a system
topics.description: System feedback can indicate whether an output meets a target and support adjustment, troubleshooting or maintenance.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 4 > Systems and Control; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: using feedback to improve a system.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They should check the measurement, water supply and system operation against the intended output.
misconceptions: A system's performance cannot be improved using information about its output.
topics.question: A plant-watering system reports that soil remains dry after running. What should its designers investigate?
topics.answer: They should check the measurement, water supply and system operation against the intended output.
topics.explanation: System feedback can indicate whether an output meets a target and support adjustment, troubleshooting or maintenance.
hints: What result was expected?
Which parts could explain the difference?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional watering system and mark an input, output, measurement and possible adjustment.

topics.name: Interacting subsystems
topics.description: A larger system can combine mechanical, electronic or digital subsystems, each contributing to a shared purpose.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 4 > Systems and Control; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: interacting subsystems.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The sensor supplies information used by a controller, which can signal the motor to move the gate.
misconceptions: Every part of a system works without affecting any other part.
topics.question: In an automatic gate, how might a sensor and motor work together?
topics.answer: The sensor supplies information used by a controller, which can signal the motor to move the gate.
topics.explanation: A larger system can combine mechanical, electronic or digital subsystems, each contributing to a shared purpose.
hints: What detects a condition?
What produces movement?
topics.activity: Sketch an automatic gate as a fictional system with sensor, controller and motor; describe one interaction.

topics.name: Selection in programs
topics.description: Selection lets a program choose an action based on a condition. A test should cover both possible outcomes.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 > Digital Technology; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: selection in programs.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Test an input where the condition is true and one where it is false, checking the intended output for each.
misconceptions: Testing one branch proves that every branch works.
topics.question: If a program says “if it is raining, show a coat”, what should be tested?
topics.answer: Test an input where the condition is true and one where it is false, checking the intended output for each.
topics.explanation: Selection lets a program choose an action based on a condition. A test should cover both possible outcomes.
hints: What happens when it is raining?
What should happen when it is not raining?
topics.activity: Write a small paper decision tree for a fictional weather message and test both branches.

topics.name: Accessibility and privacy in digital outcomes
topics.description: A digital outcome can be designed and evaluated for accessibility, privacy and responsible use of information.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 > Digital Technology; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: accessibility and privacy in digital outcomes.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It can communicate the image's purpose to people who cannot access it visually or when the image fails to load.
misconceptions: Every user experiences a digital interface in the same way.
topics.question: Why provide meaningful text for an image in an interface?
topics.answer: It can communicate the image's purpose to people who cannot access it visually or when the image fails to load.
topics.explanation: A digital outcome can be designed and evaluated for accessibility, privacy and responsible use of information.
hints: What information does the image convey?
How could that information be available in text?
topics.activity: Review a fictional webpage and write a concise text alternative for an informative image.

topics.name: Choosing materials for a purpose
topics.description: Materials behave differently when bent, pulled or exposed to water, so their properties matter to a design.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Gently compare a sheet of scrap fabric and a cardboard offcut, then draw a flexible toy cover.
evidence: Selects a flexible material and explains how its behaviour suits a cover.
misconceptions: All materials perform the same job equally well.
topics.question: Which material is likely to bend around a soft toy: a sheet of fabric or a rigid block?
topics.answer: The sheet of fabric, because it is flexible.
topics.explanation: Materials behave differently when bent, pulled or exposed to water, so their properties matter to a design.
hints: What shape must the material take?
Which choice bends easily?
topics.activity: Gently compare a sheet of scrap fabric and a cardboard offcut, then draw a flexible toy cover.
materials: teacher-provided examples or safe classroom materials as described

topics.name: Changes that can and cannot be undone
topics.description: Some material changes can be reversed, while others leave a lasting change. Cutting paper leaves pieces that do not become the original sheet just by fitting them together.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Tear a piece of scrap paper, place the pieces side by side and describe the remaining change.
evidence: Describes why the torn edges remain separate.
misconceptions: Every physical change can be undone by putting pieces together.
topics.question: Can a cut paper square become the uncut original merely by placing the pieces together?
topics.answer: No. The cut remains, even if the pieces are placed next to each other.
topics.explanation: Some material changes can be reversed, while others leave a lasting change. Cutting paper leaves pieces that do not become the original sheet just by fitting them together.
hints: What happened to the sheet?
Do the edges rejoin by themselves?
topics.activity: Tear a piece of scrap paper, place the pieces side by side and describe the remaining change.
materials: teacher-provided examples or safe classroom materials as described

topics.name: Drawing a design from different views
topics.description: A top view and a side view can show different features of the same object. A label can explain a part that is difficult to see.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Draw a small box from above and from the side; mark its height on the side view.
evidence: Identifies the height in the side view and gives a reason.
misconceptions: One drawing always reveals every feature of an object.
topics.question: Which view would best show how tall a model box is: top or side?
topics.answer: A side view, because the height is visible in that view.
topics.explanation: A top view and a side view can show different features of the same object. A label can explain a part that is difficult to see.
hints: Imagine looking across at the box.
Where can you see the vertical edge?
topics.activity: Draw a small box from above and from the side; mark its height on the side view.
materials: teacher-provided examples or safe classroom materials as described

topics.name: Clear steps and debugging
topics.description: Instructions need enough detail to be followed in the intended order. Debugging means finding and correcting a step that produces the wrong result.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Give a partner three paper-folding instructions, notice one unclear step and revise it.
evidence: Changes a specific ambiguous instruction after observing a partner follow it.
misconceptions: A vague instruction is always understood in the same way.
topics.question: An instruction says “fold” but does not say which edge to fold. What could make it clearer?
topics.answer: Name the edge and say where to fold it, then test the revised instruction.
topics.explanation: Instructions need enough detail to be followed in the intended order. Debugging means finding and correcting a step that produces the wrong result.
hints: Which information is missing?
How could a partner know which edge to use?
topics.activity: Give a partner three paper-folding instructions, notice one unclear step and revise it.
materials: teacher-provided examples or safe classroom materials as described

topics.name: Function and appearance
topics.description: A design can be judged by what it does and how it looks. The two judgements answer different questions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Build a low paper bridge and safely test it with a small eraser; sketch one change.
evidence: Explains a change using the result of the eraser test.
misconceptions: A good-looking design must also work well.
topics.question: A toy bridge looks colourful but collapses when a toy crosses. Which aspect needs improvement?
topics.answer: Its function: it needs to support the intended toy.
topics.explanation: A design can be judged by what it does and how it looks. The two judgements answer different questions.
hints: Can the toy get across?
Does the problem concern appearance or use?
topics.activity: Build a low paper bridge and safely test it with a small eraser; sketch one change.
materials: teacher-provided examples or safe classroom materials as described

topics.name: Inputs, controls and outputs
topics.description: A simple system has connected parts: an input is acted on and an output results; a control changes how the system operates.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Design, Make, and Innovate; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Draw a battery torch from the outside and label its switch and visible output; do not open the battery case.
evidence: Labels the switch and light and explains their roles.
misconceptions: A system is a single part with no interactions.

Which component creates movement?

How could one named piece of logic be reused?

What lies outside that range?

topics.answer: Accurate captions or an equivalent transcript can make the spoken information available in text.
topics.explanation: Digital media should be tested with its intended audience, considering readable text, navigation and alternatives for content in other formats.

How could it be presented as text?
topics.activity: Review a fictional video plan and add captions for its spoken instructions.

topics.explanation: AI-generated material can contain errors or bias. Designers check claims, protect private information, consider representation, and disclose use where appropriate.

Which sources and people can help verify the claim?

How could the earlier state be recovered?

topics.name: Ingredients in different foods

The same carrot can be used in each.

topics.name: Shaping and joining materials

Tape can hold the paper pieces together.

topics.name: Mixing changes food ingredients
topics.description: Mixing can combine ingredients and change how they look or feel in a food outcome.

objectives: Describe how mixing distributes differently coloured pieces through a model mixture.
evidence: Describes one visible change caused by combining ingredients.
misconceptions: Mixed ingredients always look exactly the same as they did separately.

topics.answer: Their colours and pieces can become distributed together.
topics.explanation: Mixing brings ingredients into contact and can produce a different-looking mixture without necessarily making a new substance.

Their pieces become distributed together.

topics.name: Who and what in a design brief
topics.description: A simple design brief says what is to be made and who it is for, as well as the intended situation or purpose.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Design, Make, and Innovate > Year 2 knowledge
objectives: Identify a design’s intended user, purpose and place of use from a simple brief.

The brief says it is for a classmate.

topics.name: Packaging choices and impacts
topics.description: Packaging can make a food convenient to carry while creating waste; users can compare both effects.

misconceptions: A design choice has only benefits and cannot create a problem.
topics.question: What are two things to consider when comparing single-use snack packaging with a reusable container?
topics.answer: Consider convenience for the user and the amount of waste each choice may create.
topics.explanation: A useful comparison includes how the packaging works and what happens to it after use.

Compare convenience and waste.

topics.name: Origins of materials and ingredients
topics.description: Materials and ingredients come from different sources; for example, wool comes from sheep and wheat can be milled into flour.

objectives: Match wool and flour to their animal or plant sources and describe a processing step.
evidence: Matches an everyday material or ingredient with a correct source.
misconceptions: All materials and food ingredients come directly from factories.
topics.question: Where does the wool used to make yarn come from?
topics.answer: Wool comes from animals such as sheep.
topics.explanation: A factory may process wool, but the raw fibre grows on an animal.
hints: Think about the source before the material is processed.
Sheep produce wool.
topics.activity: Make picture cards linking sheep to wool and wheat plants to flour, then add a processing step for each.

topics.name: Using feedback on a design idea
topics.description: A sketch or model can be shown to another person before making so the design can be improved.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Design, Make, and Innovate > Year 4 practices
objectives: Use feedback about stability to suggest a specific change to a design sketch.

misconceptions: Feedback is useful only after the final product is finished.
topics.question: A classmate says a sketched pencil holder may tip over. What could the designer do before making it?
topics.answer: Revise the sketch or model to try a wider base and test that idea.
topics.explanation: Feedback can reveal a possible problem while changing a sketch or model is still straightforward.
hints: What part keeps the holder stable?
Try changing the base in the sketch.
topics.activity: Sketch a paper holder, invite a classmate to comment on stability and revise the sketch to address that comment.

topics.name: Planning a making sequence

topics.answer: After the model is made.

The model needs to exist first.

topics.name: Beams and columns in structures

It is the horizontal strip.

One was folded and the other was crumpled.

What does the toy do in response?

The loose seam may be repairable.

They can become the faces of a cube.

One hand size does not represent everyone.

topics.name: Designing with community context

Ask the community rather than guessing.

Make a fold down the middle.

The structure is different.

topics.name: Marking and modelling before cutting

A paper trial can expose the error early.

topics.name: Testing wear in materials

Keep the number of strokes and rubbing surface the same.

topics.name: Ingredient roles in a food outcome

Check the flavour or tartness.

A smoother outcome usually has smaller pieces.

evidence: Distinguishes a measured mass from an opinion about flavour.

Grams are a unit of mass.

topics.name: Trialling a food design

evidence: Explains how a safe trial can reveal whether a food design meets a stated attribute.

topics.answer: The trial can show which option better meets the specification and what needs changing.
topics.explanation: A controlled small trial supplies evidence for refining the final food outcome while conserving resources.
hints: Think about checking the goal before using all the ingredients.
Compare the options on a small scale first.

A twist around an axis is torsion.

topics.question: A screw is turned and advances straight into a nut. What two motion types are involved?
topics.answer: The screw is turned with rotary motion and advances with linear motion.
topics.explanation: The threaded mechanism converts turning into movement along an axis.
hints: How does the screw turn?
How does it move along its axis?
topics.activity: Use an age-appropriate diagram or a large blunt classroom screw model to trace turning and forward motion; do not use powered tools.
materials: mechanism diagram or blunt classroom model

topics.name: Electrical and electronic functions
topics.description: Electrical components use electric energy for an output, while electronic components can process signals and control the output.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Systems and Control > Year 7 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish a controller’s decision-making role from a fan motor’s output role.
evidence: Distinguishes an output device from a control component in a simple example.
misconceptions: A motor and the controller that decides when it runs always perform the same function.
topics.question: In an automatic fan, which part decides when to turn on: the controller or the fan motor?
topics.answer: The controller makes the control decision.
topics.explanation: The motor produces movement; the controller processes information to decide when to run it.
hints: Which part produces the movement?
The controller handles the decision.
topics.activity: Label a fictional fan diagram with a controller, a power source and a motor, then describe each part's role.

topics.name: Choosing components using information
topics.description: A component's data sheet can describe values and operating limits that help a designer select it for a system.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Systems and Control > Year 8 practices
objectives: Compare a component’s maximum voltage rating with a stated supply voltage and identify the need to check other limits.
evidence: Compares a stated maximum voltage rating with a fictional circuit voltage.
misconceptions: Any electrical component is suitable for any voltage if it fits physically.
topics.question: A fictional circuit uses a 5 V supply. One part has a maximum voltage rating of 3 V and another 6 V. Which meets this limit?
topics.answer: The part with a 6 V maximum rating meets this voltage limit; other specifications must also be checked.
topics.explanation: The 5 V supply exceeds the 3 V maximum but is below the 6 V maximum. Compatibility still depends on the rest of the data sheet.
hints: Compare the 5 V supply with each maximum rating.
The supply must not exceed the maximum rating.
topics.activity: Match fictional component cards with stated design requirements; do not connect components to a power supply.

topics.name: Hardware, software and networks
topics.description: Digital systems combine physical devices, programs and connections to process or share information.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Systems and Control > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Identify hardware, software and a network connection in a digital communication example.
evidence: Identifies hardware, software and a network connection in a simple communication example.
misconceptions: A network can share information without any devices or software taking part.
topics.question: A tablet sends a message through a wireless network. Which part is hardware?
topics.answer: The tablet is hardware.
topics.explanation: The tablet is the physical device; software handles the message and the network carries information between devices.
hints: Which part can be physically held?
The tablet is the device.
topics.activity: Draw a tablet, a wireless connection and another device, and label one role of the messaging software.

topics.name: Patterns in algorithms
topics.description: Finding repeated elements in a task can make an algorithm clearer and reveal where repetition may be useful.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Digital Technology > Year 7 knowledge
objectives: Identify a repeating unit and count its occurrences in an action sequence.
evidence: Identifies a repeated action in a short set of instructions.
misconceptions: Every step in a sequence must be written differently even when actions repeat.
topics.question: In the sequence tap, clap, tap, clap, what two-action pattern repeats?
topics.answer: The pattern is tap, clap.
topics.explanation: The same two actions occur twice in the same order, so the repetition can be represented more compactly.
hints: Look at the first two actions.
Do the next two match them?
topics.activity: Write a six-action pattern, circle the repeating unit and describe how many times it occurs.

topics.name: Designing digital media for an audience
topics.description: Layout, readable text and clear organisation help a digital media outcome communicate with its intended audience.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Digital Technology > Year 7 practices
objectives: Suggest a heading layout that helps a specified audience read a digital page.
evidence: Suggests a layout choice that supports a specified reader's task.
misconceptions: A digital page works equally well for every audience without considering readability.
topics.question: A page for young readers has a tiny crowded heading. What could make the heading easier to read?
topics.answer: Use a larger, clearly spaced heading with readable contrast.
topics.explanation: Readable text and organisation help the intended audience locate and understand information.
hints: Think about the size and spacing of the heading.
Make it easier to see and separate from nearby text.
topics.activity: Sketch a simple page for a specified audience, using a clear heading and short, readable labels.

topics.name: Comparing algorithm growth
topics.description: Algorithms solving the same problem can be compared by how the number of steps or memory use grows as input size increases.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Digital Technology > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Compare supplied step counts at different input sizes to identify which algorithm grows faster in the example.
evidence: Uses a supplied table to compare how two algorithms' step counts change with input size.
misconceptions: The algorithm with the shortest name is always the most efficient.
topics.question: For input sizes 10 and 20, algorithm A takes 10 and 20 steps; B takes 100 and 400. Which grows faster in this example?
topics.answer: Algorithm B's step count grows faster.
topics.explanation: B's steps rise from 100 to 400, while A's rise from 10 to 20; this table is evidence for the stated sizes.
hints: Compare how much each step count changes.
B quadruples while A doubles.
topics.activity: Make a table of the supplied step counts and sketch how each changes as input size grows.

topics.name: Testing and communicating design limits
topics.description: Responsible development includes testing an outcome, identifying risks and telling users about known limitations.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Design, Make, and Innovate > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Record a prototype’s test conditions and communicate an untested load or other limitation.
evidence: Identifies both a test and a limitation to communicate before a prototype is used.
misconceptions: A prototype with an attractive appearance needs no testing or information about its limits.
topics.question: A paper shelf model has only been tested with one small load. What should the designer tell a user?
topics.answer: State that it has only been tested with that small load and should not be assumed safe for heavier loads.
topics.explanation: A clear limitation prevents a test result from being treated as evidence for untested conditions.
hints: What has actually been tested?
The heavier-load performance is not established.
topics.activity: Write a short test note for a fictional model, listing the load used, what happened and one untested condition.

topics.name: Intellectual property and design reuse
topics.description: Intellectual property rights and permissions affect how designs, media and other outcomes may be used or shared.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Design, Make, and Innovate > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Check permission, licence conditions and attribution before reusing a design.
evidence: Explains why credit and permission are separate questions when reusing a design.
misconceptions: Naming a creator always gives permission to copy and share their work.
topics.question: Before reusing a designer's image, what should a learner check besides naming the creator?
topics.answer: Check the permission or licence and its conditions.
topics.explanation: Attribution identifies the creator; the licence or permission determines which uses are allowed and on what terms.
hints: Does credit itself state permission?
Check the licence or ask for permission.
topics.activity: Read two fictional licence summaries and decide which permits a stated classroom reuse, then record the required attribution.

topics.name: Crating a product sketch
topics.description: Crating uses a simple enclosing shape as a guide for proportions and perspective before detail is added.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Spatial and Product Design > Year 9 practices
objectives: Use a light construction box to guide a product sketch’s proportions before adding its final outline.
evidence: Explains the role of a construction box in a three-dimensional sketch.
misconceptions: Construction lines are the finished product outline and must all remain equally dark.
topics.question: Why might a designer draw a light box around a product idea before adding detail?
topics.answer: The box helps organise the product's size, proportions and perspective.
topics.explanation: A simple construction shape gives a guide for placing details; lighter guide lines can be distinguished from the final outline.
hints: Think about the product's overall shape first.
The light box acts as a proportion guide.
topics.activity: Lightly sketch a box around a fictional desk organiser, then add its main shape and darken the final outline.

topics.name: Paraline design drawings
topics.description: A paraline drawing depicts a three-dimensional design using distinct axis directions. Edges following the same direction stay parallel, and measurements are represented along the axes.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Spatial and Product Design > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Identify edges that remain parallel in a paraline drawing and distinguish them from converging perspective lines.
evidence: Identifies a pair of parallel edges in each axis direction and distinguishes them from converging perspective lines.
misconceptions: All three-dimensional design drawings must use lines that converge toward a vanishing point.
topics.question: In a paraline drawing, what happens to edges that follow the same axis direction?
topics.answer: They remain parallel in the drawing.
topics.explanation: Edges following the same axis direction remain parallel. The different axis directions are distinct; perspective drawings can instead show parallel edges converging.
hints: Look at lines that follow one axis.
They stay parallel.
topics.activity: Sketch a simple paraline box using three distinct, non-parallel axis directions. Mark a matching pair of parallel edges in each direction.

topics.name: Rendering light and form
topics.description: Rendering can use light and shade to communicate the form of a three-dimensional design idea.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Spatial and Product Design > Year 9 practices
objectives: Shade visible surfaces consistently with one chosen light source.
evidence: Places light and shadow consistently with one chosen light source.
misconceptions: Light and shade in a drawing have no relationship to the direction of the light source.
topics.question: If a light shines on the left side of a box, which side would generally be lighter?
topics.answer: The side facing the light, on the left, would generally be lighter.
topics.explanation: The light source helps determine which surfaces receive more light and which are in shade.
hints: Which side faces the light?
The side facing it is generally lighter.
topics.activity: Draw a box, mark one light source and shade the surfaces consistently; avoid looking directly into any bright light.

topics.name: Third-angle projected views
topics.description: Third-angle projection arranges standard orthographic views so that the top view is placed above the front view.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Spatial and Product Design > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Place a top view above a front view in a third-angle orthographic layout.
evidence: Correctly places the top view relative to the front view in a third-angle layout.
misconceptions: A set of projected views can be arranged randomly without affecting how readers interpret it.
topics.question: In a third-angle layout, where is the top view normally placed relative to the front view?
topics.answer: Above the front view.
topics.explanation: Consistent view placement lets readers interpret how the separate projections relate to the same object.
hints: Identify the front view first.
Place the top view above it.
topics.activity: Draw front, top and right-side views of a simple block and arrange them in a labelled third-angle layout.

topics.name: Unconventional material choices
topics.description: A designer can consider an unfamiliar or repurposed material for a task, then test whether it meets the design requirements.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Materials Technology (Resistant and Textiles) > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Identify a relevant test for an alternative material against a stated protection requirement.
evidence: Suggests a relevant test before using an unconventional material in an outcome.
misconceptions: A repurposed material is always suitable merely because it is available.
topics.question: A designer considers clean fabric offcuts for protective wrapping. What should be checked?
topics.answer: Test whether the offcuts provide the needed protection and suit the user and intended conditions.
topics.explanation: An unusual or reused material must still meet the outcome's performance and safety requirements.
hints: What must the wrapping protect?
Test whether the fabric performs that function.
topics.activity: Use a fictional brief and two clean material samples to list protection, durability and user requirements before making a choice.

topics.name: Accurate measuring and marking
topics.description: Accurate measurements and clear marks help material parts fit their intended dimensions before shaping or joining.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Materials Technology (Resistant and Textiles) > Year 9 practices
objectives: Measure and check a 10 cm mark against a stated size requirement.
evidence: Checks a marked dimension against a stated specification.
misconceptions: A small marking error can never affect how parts fit together.
topics.question: Why check a 10 cm mark before cutting a piece intended to fit a 10 cm space?
topics.answer: A measurement error could make the part too short or too long to fit.
topics.explanation: Checking the mark against the specification can reveal an error before material is permanently changed.
hints: What happens if the part is the wrong length?
It may not fit the intended space.
topics.activity: Measure and mark a 10 cm line on scrap paper, then use a ruler to check it before any cutting.

topics.name: Using test evidence to refine materials
topics.description: Testing candidate materials and construction methods can reveal whether they meet a specification before final production.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Materials Technology (Resistant and Textiles) > Year 10 practices
objectives: Use test results to choose a material for a stated flexibility requirement.
evidence: Uses a test result to select a material for a stated requirement.
misconceptions: The material that looks best must always meet every functional requirement.
topics.question: A brief requires a pouch fabric that bends easily. One tested sample is flexible and another cracks when folded. Which is more suitable on that criterion?
topics.answer: The flexible sample is more suitable for the bending requirement.
topics.explanation: The comparison provides evidence about flexibility, although other requirements should also be checked.
hints: Focus on what happened when each sample was folded.
The flexible one meets the stated bending criterion.
topics.activity: Compare two fictional material test cards against a pouch brief, choose one and name a further test needed.

topics.name: Emulsification as processing
topics.description: Emulsification disperses one liquid in another that would otherwise tend to separate, producing a mixture with different observable qualities.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Food and Processing Technology > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Describe an emulsion as droplets of one liquid dispersed through another.
evidence: Identifies emulsification as a way to disperse droplets of one liquid in another.
misconceptions: Oil and water always form a permanent uniform mixture without mixing or an emulsifier.
topics.question: What is an emulsion in a food-processing context?
topics.answer: It is a mixture in which droplets of one liquid are dispersed through another.
topics.explanation: Some liquids tend to separate, so mixing and suitable ingredients can affect the mixture's texture and stability.
hints: Think about small droplets spread through another liquid.
An emulsion disperses one liquid through another.
topics.activity: Observe a sealed clear bottle of water and oil before and after gently shaking; do not open or taste it.
materials: sealed clear bottle containing water and oil

topics.name: Preventing food cross-contamination
topics.description: Food safety planning includes preventing harmful material or allergens from moving between foods through hands, equipment or surfaces.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Food and Processing Technology > Year 9 practices
objectives: Plan separate clean utensils to reduce allergen transfer between foods.
evidence: Identifies a safer action when a used utensil could transfer an allergen to another food.
misconceptions: Food is automatically safe if an allergen is not listed as an intended ingredient.
topics.question: A spoon used for peanut butter is about to be used for a peanut-free food. What should happen?
topics.answer: Use a clean utensil and follow the school's allergen procedures.
topics.explanation: Residue on shared equipment can transfer an allergen even when it is not an intended ingredient.
hints: What might remain on the used spoon?
Use a clean utensil and follow the procedure.
topics.activity: Sort fictional utensil and ingredient cards to plan separate, clean work areas; do not use real allergens.

topics.name: Food processing and resource use
topics.description: Processing choices can affect consistency, yield, labour and energy use as well as the final food's qualities.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Food and Processing Technology > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Compare processing options by time and waste alongside the required food quality.
evidence: Compares processing options using both a production measure and a quality requirement.
misconceptions: The fastest process is automatically the best regardless of waste or food quality.
topics.question: Two fictional methods make the same snack; one is faster but produces more waste. What should be compared?
topics.answer: Compare the time saved and extra waste alongside quality and user needs.
topics.explanation: A fit-for-purpose decision weighs several outcomes, not just speed.
hints: What is gained and what is lost?
Compare speed, waste and the required quality.
topics.activity: Read two fictional process-result cards and select a method for a brief that specifies quality and a waste target.

topics.name: Stopping a repeated instruction
topics.description: A repeated instruction can continue while a condition is true and stop when that condition changes.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Digital Technology > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Trace a loop’s counter and identify when its condition first becomes false.
evidence: Explains when a simple loop stops from a stated condition.
misconceptions: Every loop must run forever once it begins.
topics.question: A counter starts at 0. A loop moves while the counter is less than 3 and increases it by 1 each time. When does it stop?
topics.answer: It stops when the counter reaches 3.
topics.explanation: The counter progresses from 0 to 1, 2 and 3; at 3 the condition is false and the loop stops.
hints: What happens to the counter each time?
The loop stops when the counter is no longer less than 3.
topics.activity: Trace the counter values in a fictional loop starting at 0 and mark the first value that makes the condition false.

topics.name: Testing friction in a mechanism
topics.description: Friction and alignment can affect how well a mechanical system moves; a controlled test can help identify a fault.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Systems and Control > Year 9 practices
objectives: Locate a suspected rubbing point and suggest an alignment change to test.
evidence: Suggests a way to compare movement after changing one suspected cause.
misconceptions: A mechanism that moves poorly must always have an electrical fault.
topics.question: A paper wheel rubs against its frame and turns poorly. What mechanical issue should be checked?
topics.answer: Check whether the wheel is misaligned and rubbing against the frame.
topics.explanation: Contact and friction can resist movement; correcting the alignment may improve the system.
hints: Look at where the wheel touches the frame.
Rubbing at that contact may slow it.
topics.activity: Use a paper wheel-and-frame sketch to mark the rubbing point and propose an alignment change; do not use powered equipment.

topics.name: Microcontrollers in control systems
topics.description: A microcontroller can read a sensor, follow programmed instructions and control an output in an integrated system.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Systems and Control > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain how a microcontroller uses a sensor input to control an output.
evidence: Identifies the processing role of a controller between a sensor and an output.
misconceptions: A sensor alone contains every decision and mechanical output in a controlled system.
topics.question: In an automated light, what can read the sensor and decide whether to switch the light on?
topics.answer: A programmed microcontroller or controller can make that decision.
topics.explanation: The sensor supplies an input; the controller processes it and sends a command to the output.
hints: Find the part between sensing and switching.
The controller processes the input.
topics.activity: Draw a block diagram linking a light sensor, microcontroller decision and lamp output; use a simulation or paper only.

topics.name: Testing a control threshold
topics.description: A sensor-based system can compare a measured value with a threshold and use the result to control an output.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Systems and Control > Year 10 practices
objectives: Predict the output for values below, at and above a specified threshold.
evidence: Uses two test values on either side of a threshold to predict a control response.
misconceptions: Testing only one input proves that every possible sensor value is handled correctly.
topics.question: A model turns a lamp on when light level is below 20. What should happen at a level of 15?
topics.answer: The lamp should turn on.
topics.explanation: Fifteen is below the threshold of 20; another test should check a value at or above the threshold.
hints: Compare 15 with 20.
Fifteen is less than 20.
topics.activity: On paper, test the fictional rule at 15, 20 and 25 and record the expected lamp state for each.

topics.name: Actuators and other outputs
topics.description: An actuator converts electrical energy into mechanical movement, while another output device may produce light or sound instead.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Systems and Control > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish a movement-producing actuator from output devices that emit light or sound.
evidence: Identifies a motor as an actuator that produces movement.
misconceptions: Every electrical output is an actuator even when it produces no movement.
topics.question: Which output is an actuator that produces movement: a motor or an indicator lamp?
topics.answer: The motor.
topics.explanation: A motor can convert electrical energy into mechanical movement; an indicator lamp produces light.
hints: Which output moves something?
The motor produces movement.
topics.activity: Sort fictional output cards into mechanical movement, light and sound, then identify the actuators.

topics.name: Tracing program values
topics.description: A trace table records how variables change as instructions run, helping find errors in an algorithm.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Digital Technology > Year 9 practices
objectives: Record a variable’s starting value and successive updates in a trace table.
evidence: Traces a variable through repeated additions and records the final value.
misconceptions: A variable keeps its first value even when a program assigns a new value.
topics.question: A variable starts at 2 and increases by 3 twice. What value does it have at the end?
topics.answer: It has the value 8.
topics.explanation: After the first increase it is 5; after the second it is 8.
hints: Work through one increase at a time.
The values are 2, then 5, then 8.
topics.activity: Create a three-row trace table for the starting value and each update, then check the final value.

topics.name: Readable program names
topics.description: Meaningful variable and function names help people understand and maintain a program.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Digital Technology > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Choose descriptive variable names that communicate their roles in a program.
evidence: Chooses a name that describes a value's role in a simple program.
misconceptions: Short or random names are always easier to understand than descriptive names.
topics.question: Which name better communicates a price total: totalPrice or x?
topics.answer: totalPrice better describes the value's role.
topics.explanation: A descriptive name makes the program easier to read and revisit, especially when there are several values.
hints: Which name tells you what the value represents?
totalPrice describes the total.
topics.activity: Rename three fictional variables so each name describes its role, then explain one choice.

topics.name: Hexadecimal representation
topics.description: Hexadecimal is a base-16 representation that uses digits 0–9 and letters A–F for the values 10–15.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Digital Technology > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Match selected hexadecimal digits, including A and F, with their decimal values.
evidence: Interprets a single hexadecimal digit as a decimal value.
misconceptions: In hexadecimal, A stands for an unknown variable rather than a digit value.
topics.question: What decimal value does the hexadecimal digit A represent?
topics.answer: It represents 10.
topics.explanation: After 9, hexadecimal uses A, B, C, D, E and F for the values 10 to 15.
hints: Hexadecimal has more digit symbols than decimal.
A is the first value after 9.
topics.activity: Make a matching chart for hexadecimal digits 9, A, B and F with their decimal values.

topics.name: Digital colour values
topics.description: A digital colour can be represented by values for red, green and blue, including hexadecimal values.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Digital Technology > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Identify which colour component is at its maximum in a given hexadecimal RGB code.
evidence: Identifies the red component in a stated RGB colour code.
misconceptions: A hexadecimal colour code is a word describing a colour with no numeric components.
topics.question: In the RGB code #FF0000, which colour component is at its maximum?
topics.answer: The red component is at its maximum.
topics.explanation: The first pair represents red and FF is the maximum two-digit hexadecimal value; green and blue are both zero.
hints: Read the pairs in red, green, blue order.
The first pair is FF.
topics.activity: On paper, label the red, green and blue pairs in #FF0000 and #00FF00 and compare them.

topics.name: Interactive and time-based media
topics.description: Digital media can be interactive, information-based or time-based, with design choices suited to the audience and format.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Digital Technology > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Recognise time-based video and compare its design needs with an information page and an interactive quiz.
evidence: Identifies a video that plays over time as time-based media.
misconceptions: Every digital outcome is interactive in the same way.
topics.question: A recorded video plays from beginning to end over two minutes. What type of media is it?
topics.answer: It is time-based media.
topics.explanation: Its content unfolds over a duration, even though a player may also provide controls.
hints: Does the content unfold across a period of time?
The video has a duration.
topics.activity: Compare a fictional video, information page and interactive quiz, and describe a design need for each.

Reading different views of a design prepares learners to connect a flat net with its three-dimensional form.
A measurable specification can use ergonomic information to judge whether an outcome fits its intended users.
Identifying users and constraints provides a foundation for asking how community context affects the design.
Comparing construction and joining techniques helps learners identify when a fold can create a useful shape.
Knowing material properties such as flexibility prepares learners to investigate how structure affects those properties.
Testing a model before committing resources supports checking a material template against its specification.
A fair comparison of material properties provides the method for investigating wear under repeated use.
Identifying sensory attributes gives designers a way to select ingredients that contribute those attributes.
Understanding that ingredients and methods affect food qualities helps learners predict a texture from a particular method.
A sensory profile provides one kind of evidence that can be compared with objective measurements.
Understanding controlled processing conditions helps learners interpret a small trial comparing food options.
Understanding tension and compression provides a basis for comparing additional ways forces act on structures.
Distinguishing rotary from linear motion enables learners to describe how a mechanism can connect them.
Recognising input, process and output helps separate the roles of a controller and an output device.
Reading a system diagram identifies the component whose specifications must be checked for the intended role.
Identifying inputs, processing and outputs helps learners see how devices and connections share work in a digital system.
Knowing that algorithms are ordered instructions helps learners identify and describe repeating parts of a sequence.
Thinking about how a design works as well as how it looks supports decisions about readable digital layouts.
Recognising repeated work helps learners compare how the number of algorithm steps grows with larger inputs.
Identifying hazards and controls prepares learners to communicate the limits of a test or prototype.
Recognising creators and source permissions supports more detailed decisions about design reuse and intellectual property.
A perspective sketch shows a three-dimensional form; crating provides a guide for constructing it with consistent proportions.
Knowing one way to represent depth helps learners compare perspective drawing with parallel-axis representation.
A proportioned construction sketch provides a form on which light and shade can be represented.
Recognising front, top and side projections prepares learners to arrange those views using a drawing convention.
Understanding performance properties allows a designer to test an unconventional material against the same requirements as a conventional one.
A measurable specification provides the dimension against which a mark can be checked.
Recognising relevant material properties makes it possible to interpret test evidence against a design requirement.
Understanding that processing can change a food's qualities prepares learners to examine how dispersing liquids affects a mixture.
Identifying allergen requirements helps learners plan handling practices that prevent accidental transfer.
Recognising processing trade-offs prepares learners to include yield, time and resource use in a reasoned comparison.
Counting a fixed repetition prepares learners to reason about repetition controlled by a stopping condition.
Knowing how a mechanism moves helps learners identify where unwanted contact and friction may affect it.
Distinguishing sensing from action helps learners place the programmed controller between input and output.
Understanding feedback and target values supports checking how a system responds around a control threshold.
Recognising a sensor and actuator in a system enables a closer comparison of movement with other output types.
Understanding that a variable can hold changing values prepares learners to record those changes in a trace.
Knowing that variables store values makes it useful to name them according to their roles.
Experience representing numbers with place-value systems helps learners compare base two with base sixteen.
Understanding hexadecimal digits makes it possible to interpret the component values in a colour code.
Considering a media outcome's audience and layout prepares learners to compare conventions for different media formats.
